title: Shabbat renews it
hook: for the Sefat Emet, each Shabbat renews that inner point
tomorrow: can God's will hide inside a human mistake?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sefat Emet's inner point: covered by the week's layers, never stained. The inner point. Today, the day he says it comes back.

Some weeks a day off doesn't fix anything. You sleep in, scroll, and still feel drained by Sunday night. The Torah has a strange word about rest. Exodus thirty-one, on the Sabbath: in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh He rested, and then one more word, vayinafash, usually put into English as and was refreshed. The rabbis hear nefesh in it, soul. So, the odd detail: why would the Torah say God needed refreshing? And why say it about the Sabbath?
screen: `A DAY OFF THAT DOESN'T FIX IT.` → `HE RESTED, AND WAS REFRESHED.` → `WHY WOULD GOD NEED THAT?`

segments.voice: The Talmud takes the odd word seriously. Resh Lakish says that on Shabbat a person is given an extra soul, a neshamah yeteirah, and when Shabbat ends it's taken back. He hears the word as a sigh: vay, avdah nefesh, woe, the soul is gone. So the refreshing in the verse turns out to be ours. Something is added on the seventh day that the week doesn't give. Now the Sefat Emet, yesterday's teacher, picks up the thread. All week, he teaches, the inner point gets covered by work and noise. Shabbat is when it's renewed, when the point comes back to itself, and the coming week draws its life from that day. So in his reading Shabbat isn't a break from the week. It's the week's source. The puzzle solved: the verse speaks of refreshing so that we'd know the seventh day renews the soul, not only the body. That's why Shabbat has its own way of doing things: not making, not fixing, not finishing. What you stop doing makes room for the point to come back. Even the goodbye carries it. At Havdalah, as Shabbat ends, people smell sweet spices, and one reason given is that they comfort the soul as the extra one leaves.
screen: `VAYINAFASH: AND WAS REFRESHED.` · `AN EXTRA SOUL, TAKEN BACK.` · `THE POINT COMES BACK TO ITSELF.` · `THE WEEK'S SOURCE, NOT A BREAK.` · then, large: `SHABBAT RENEWS.`

segments.voice: Set your phone face-down, out of reach if you can. Sit back, let your hands rest open on your knees, and stop doing anything at all for the sit: no fixing, no planning, no finishing. Let it be a small taste of the seventh day, and notice what comes back to you when nothing is being made.
Shabbat renews it: for the Sefat Emet, each Shabbat makes the inner point new, and the coming week draws its life from that day.
One line for the week: shabbat renews, so the seventh day is a source, not a gap. Until next time.

howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat stop weekday work from Friday sunset to Saturday night, with candles, wine and challah, prayer and rest, and close it with Havdalah, blessing wine, sweet spices and a braided candle.

sources.ref: Exodus 31:17 (on the seventh day He ceased from work and rested; vayinafash)
Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 16a (Resh Lakish: an extra soul is given on Shabbat and taken back at its end; vay, avdah nefesh)
Sefat Emet (Rabbi Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter of Ger), teachings on Shabbat: the inner point renewed; the week blessed from Shabbat
Havdalah spices as comfort for the departing extra soul (a reason given by medieval commentators on Beitzah 33b / Pesachim 102b)

notes: Exodus 31:17 paraphrased; 'and was refreshed' is the common English rendering, given without quotation marks. 'The rabbis hear nefesh in it' rests on Beitzah 16a's wordplay (vay, avdah nefesh); the lesson makes no independent etymology claim. Confirm.
Beitzah 16a (also Taanit 27b) paraphrased: Resh Lakish on the neshamah yeteirah. Confirm attribution.

Sefat Emet on Shabbat renewing the inner point and the week drawing its life from Shabbat: paraphrased as a theme of his Shabbat teachings; please cite one passage. The 'blessing of the week from Shabbat' also echoes the Zohar.
Havdalah spices: 'one reason given' is that they comfort the soul as the extra soul departs (Tosafot and others); confirm the source reference.
Puzzle shape: the odd detail is a verse saying God was refreshed. Practice kind: body posture (phone down, hands open). Not eyes-closed.
